section_summary: This section centers on Kilsoo Haan (also writing as W. K. Lyhan), representing the Sino-Korean People's League, and his 1935–1936 appeals for official investigations into alleged Japanese propaganda and “Japanization” in Hawaii. It includes a lengthy petition concerning schools, cultural organizations, dual citizenship and Pacific strategy; State Department annotations; correspondence with Hawaiian educators who rejected Haan's charges; and newspaper clippings offered as supporting evidence. Additional clippings document Japanese training-ship visits, visiting lecturers, university programs, cultural funding and changes within the Japanese Council of the Institute of Pacific Relations.

subfiles.title: Composite clipping page: “Five Japanese Ships to Call” and an incomplete letter-to-the-editor fragment
subfiles.about: Reports scheduled visits by Japanese training ships to Hawaiian ports, alongside a later incomplete fragment referring to responsibility for Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.summary: The principal article lists Japanese merchant-marine and navigation-school vessels expected at Honolulu, Hilo and Kahului, naming several captains and itineraries. A separate fragment at the top begins in mid-thought with a reference to Pearl Harbor and a letter to the editor. The sheet bears a February 6, 1942 filing stamp, although the ship article is dated July 12, 1939.

subfiles.title: Identification or routing slip for Grant Smith
subfiles.about: A nearly blank administrative slip bearing Grant Smith's name and filing marks.
subfiles.summary: The page contains little substantive text beyond a date heading or filing notation and the name Grant Smith. It appears to be an identification, routing or separation sheet within the file.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Haan's correspondence
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Recommends that another letter from the writer using the name Ly Haan not be acknowledged.
subfiles.summary: The brief internal note says the letter contains nothing new or important. Its author concludes that further letters from the writer, whose usual pen name is rendered as Ly Haan, should not be acknowledged.

subfiles.title: Letter from Kilsoo Haan to Secretary Hull enclosing a petition and “People's Preparedness”
subfiles.to: Cordell A. Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a petition seeking an inquiry into alleged Japanese activities in Hawaii and describes warnings Haan said he had received.
subfiles.summary: Haan encloses a Sino-Korean People's League petition to Hawaii's legislature and a translation of the tract “People's Preparedness.” He alleges that Japanese propaganda was being distributed in Hawaii and says consular secretary G. Masuo repeatedly warned him. Haan emphasizes his loyalty to the United States, expresses fear of arrest or extradition to Korea and asks Hull to act justly if reprisals occur.

subfiles.title: “People's Preparedness”
subfiles.from: Japanese Naval Press Bureau (attributed by the covering letter)
subfiles.about: Argues for Japanese national strength, military preparedness and rejection of unequal naval limitations.
subfiles.summary: The tract rejects reliance on international friendship or the League of Nations and maintains that justice is respected only when backed by national power. It treats Japan's position in Manchuria as evidence of the need for self-reliance and stronger defenses. It characterizes the Washington and London naval agreements as unequal and calls for national unity during the Shōwa era.

subfiles.title: Petition to the 1935 Territorial Legislature concerning “Japanization” in Hawaii
subfiles.from: W. K. Lyhan, representative of the Sino-Korean People's League in Hawaii
subfiles.to: Senate and House of Representatives, 1935 regular session of the Territorial Legislature of Hawaii
subfiles.about: Requests a legislative inquiry into alleged Japanese educational, cultural and political influence in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The petition alleges that Japan sought to influence Hawaiian public education through textbooks, reference works, visual materials and cultural organizations. It cites Japanese officials and intellectuals, criticizes language schools and Buddhist institutions, and argues that dual citizenship and consular registration weakened Americanization. The document also surveys Japanese expansion in Asia and the Pacific, presenting Hawaii as strategically vulnerable. It concludes by asking legislators to investigate and restrain institutions said to foster Japanese loyalty among American-born residents.

subfiles.title: State Department routing annotation on Haan's letter and photostat
subfiles.about: Calls the latter portion of Haan's letter interesting but describes enclosure 6 as apparently phony.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten annotation directs two officials' attention to the section beginning with item K and to enclosure 6, described as a photostat. A second comment says, “The photostat looks phony,” recording immediate skepticism about Haan's purported evidence.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. K. Lyhan to Secretary Hull on alleged Japanese cultural propaganda
subfiles.to: Cordell A. Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Urges a federal investigation of alleged Japanese cultural and educational influence in Hawaii and requests financial support for continued monitoring.
subfiles.summary: Lyhan claims that Japan's Foreign Office directed a network of cultural, educational, religious and consular bodies intended to influence American opinion and Japanese Americans. He alleges that Japan planned eventual attacks on Hawaii and Alaska and presents textbooks, visiting professors, language schools, scholarships and lectures as parts of the program. Particular emphasis is placed on a purported letter from Setsuichi Aoki to Wilfred Tsukiyama, which Lyhan treats as confirmation of his claims. He closes by asking for financial aid and lists fourteen supporting enclosures.

subfiles.title: Letter from Kilsoo Haan to University of Hawaii president David L. Crawford
subfiles.to: David L. Crawford, president of the University of Hawaii
subfiles.about: Objects to a university course designed for Japanese-language-school teachers and alleges that it assists Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Haan quotes Takie Okumura, Shinryu Umehara, Inazo Nitobe, Kikujiro Ishii, Setsuichi Aoki and Keisuke Okada to argue that Japanese language schools promoted Japanese national spirit. He connects the university, the Institute of Pacific Relations and public education officials to the disputed “Textbook on Japan.” He further alleges that Professor Royama acknowledged being sent by Japan's Cultural Bureau and warns that cultural programs could shape future American voters in Japan's favor.

subfiles.title: Arthur L. Dean's reply to Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.about: Rejects Haan's accusation that Hawaiian educational institutions were cooperating in Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Dean recalls an earlier unsuccessful effort to regulate Japanese language schools but brands Haan's broader charges false. He distinguishes studying and appreciating a culture from approving a government's policies, using German language, scholarship and music as an analogy. He concludes that Haan's argument appears driven more by Korean hostility toward Japan than by concern for American security.

subfiles.title: Charles R. Hemenway's reply to Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.about: Dismisses Haan's charge against the University of Hawaii and defends cultural understanding.
subfiles.summary: Hemenway calls the allegation that the University of Hawaii was promoting Japanization “utterly absurd.” He argues that international friendliness and mutual respect depend upon knowledge and understanding. He characterizes Haan's rhetoric as a “Hymn of Hate” conflicting with American ideals.

subfiles.title: Letter from Kilsoo Haan to Oren E. Long
subfiles.to: Oren E. Long, superintendent of public instruction
subfiles.about: Criticizes Long's pacifism and educational policies toward Japanese-descended pupils and disputes the treatment of Mrs. Haan.
subfiles.summary: Haan argues that Long's pacifism and alleged accommodation of Japanese institutions endangered American security. He makes sweeping claims about the loyalties of Japanese-descended children, citing their play, language-school environment and admiration for Japanese figures. The letter also disputes Long's earlier statements about teachers and alleges that Mrs. Haan was treated unfairly in an appointment decision.

subfiles.title: “Give Them the Truth”
subfiles.about: Publishes and endorses Lyhan's claims after another Honolulu newspaper allegedly declined his letter.
subfiles.summary: The editorial responds to a statehood controversy involving J. R. Mahaffy and Julia Gatton and criticizes the Honolulu Star-Bulletin's demand for an honest presentation of facts. It reproduces Lyhan's quotations from Theodore Roosevelt and several Japanese figures to argue that Japanese organizations cultivated dual loyalty and national spirit in Hawaii. The newspaper asks whether leading Americans were indirectly assisting Japanization under the banners of peace and internationalism.

subfiles.title: “Japan Illustrates Her Own Ambitions”
subfiles.about: Uses the design on Japanese wrapping material as purported evidence of ideas of world domination.
subfiles.summary: The item reproduces Japanese characters and a globe design reportedly found on a kimono parcel purchased in Kobe. Its caption interprets the wrapper as evidence that Japanese jingoists were disseminating ideas of world domination to their citizens.

subfiles.title: Composite clippings on Rikio Sugano, Tokushi Suhara, Ryokai Fukui and Frederick William Walker
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese visitors and lectures, Sugano's exclusion from the United States, and an unrelated plantation engineer's death.
subfiles.summary: One clipping announces explorer Rikio Sugano's planned lectures on Manchukuo and Mongolia, while another reports that he was barred from admission because of an earlier appeal for loyalty to Japan among people of Japanese ancestry. A separate article describes education representative Tokushi Suhara's goodwill mission to invite American teachers to Japan and notes the arrival of Buddhist priest Ryokai Fukui. The page also contains an unrelated obituary for plantation engineer Frederick William Walker.

subfiles.title: Composite clippings on Eiichi Kiyooka and a Japanese cultural gift to the University of Hawaii
subfiles.about: Reports Kiyooka's visiting professorship and a 20,000-yen Japanese cultural grant for University of Hawaii library books.
subfiles.summary: The first article says Eiichi Kiyooka arrived from Keio University to teach Japanese cultural history, modern leaders and methods for Japanese-language-school teachers. The second describes a 20,000-yen gift from Japan's Cultural Bureau to purchase thousands of books for the University of Hawaii's Oriental Institute. It credits consular officials and retired banker Masusaku Nakamura with assisting the project.

subfiles.title: “Kiyooka Writing Child's History”
subfiles.about: Describes Eiichi Kiyooka's planned history of Japan for young American readers.
subfiles.summary: Kiyooka says he is writing a simple history of Japan intended primarily for American children about ten years old. The work begins with Amaterasu and the Kojiki, proceeds from mythology through modern history and will include explanatory comments. He hopes to publish it in America before or after returning to Japan in September.

subfiles.title: Nippu Jiji page containing articles on FERA, Nanjing finance and Viscount Ishii
subfiles.about: Combines local relief news, commentary on China's currency problems and notice of Kikujiro Ishii's appointment to the Japanese Council of the Institute of Pacific Relations.
subfiles.summary: A local article reports that Hawaii's FERA work-relief program might end around June 30 as workers shifted toward PWA, highway, military and naval projects. Masaji Yoshida's financial commentary discusses Nanjing's monetary reform, deflation, silver reserves and the possible effects of changes in American silver purchasing. Another article announces Viscount Kikujiro Ishii as chairman of the Japanese Council of the Institute of Pacific Relations following its merger with the International Association of Japan and lists the council's executive committee.
